Maria: Finished my essay draft on urban water policy!
Kiran: Nice. Did you send it to the chatbot to fix it?
Maria: Nope. I wrote all of it first. Then I told the tool: don't rewrite anything, just point out where my reasoning has holes
Kiran: And?
Maria: Three. One, I jumped from "pipes are old" to "privatise them" with nothing in between. Two, I never said who pays. Three, my last paragraph says something my first one denies 😅
Kiran: Ouch
Maria: But I fixed all three myself tonight. It's still my essay, just tighter 🙂

qa.q: How many gaps did the tool point out in Maria's draft?
How does Maria feel about the tool's feedback, and what tells you so?
qa.a: Maria feels relieved and pleased, since the essay is still Maria's own and, as the chat says, just tighter.

qa.q: What could Maria do if one of the gaps cannot be fixed alone, and why?
qa.a: Maria could ask a classmate for another view, because a gap in reasoning sometimes needs information Maria does not have.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Maria's plan compared with letting the tool write it?
qa.a: Kiran may be impressed that Maria kept authorship, and might try the same critique approach for a draft of Kiran's own.

grounding: A student writes a draft, asks the tool to find gaps in reasoning, and fixes them personally.

subtype: Approach: ask the tool to critique rather than write [Thinking]
passage:
The power in Shreya's village came back at eight, and she went straight to the laptop on the charpai. Her agriculture college report on drip irrigation in her father's fields was drafted, all five pages, typed over a week.
Tanvir, who ran the phone shop in the market and had helped her set up the chatbot, had told her, "Just ask it to write the conclusion." She thought about it. If it writes the conclusion, the examiner reads its thinking, not mine. And I'm the one who saw the fields.
So she pasted her draft and typed: "Don't rewrite anything. List the gaps in my reasoning." The tool said she claimed water savings without saying how she measured them, and ignored the cost of pipes.
She added her notes on the bucket measurements from April and a paragraph on pipe cost, in her own words. The report was longer now, and every line was still hers.

qa.q: What did the tool say Shreya had left out?
qa.a: She claimed water savings without saying how she measured them, and ignored the cost of pipes.

qa.q: Why did Shreya decide not to let the tool write her conclusion, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She felt protective of her own work, reasoning that the examiner should read her thinking, since she was the one who saw the fields.

qa.q: What else could Shreya do with the tool's list of gaps?
qa.a: She could also ask her teacher to review the fixed version, since a person who knows the subject can confirm the gaps are really closed.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Shreya's choice?
qa.a: Tanvir might think it is slower than his suggestion, but he could also see that her report stayed her own and got stronger.

grounding: Shows a student drafting a report and asking the tool only for gaps in reasoning, then fixing them personally to keep authorship.

subtype: Approach: ask the tool to critique rather than write [Thinking]

Chen had written the philosophy essay on a Saturday in the Vancouver public library, three pages arguing that promises bind even when breaking them helps more people. It felt solid. Too solid, maybe.
Clara, from the same seminar, leaned over. "Get the bot to write the counter-argument section. It's good at that."
Chen shook his head. "Then it's the bot arguing with me. I want to know what I missed."
He pasted the essay and typed: "Don't write anything for me. What's the strongest objection I haven't answered, and where is my reasoning weakest?" The tool pointed out that he never defined what counts as a promise, and that his second example assumed what it was trying to prove.
Chen winced, opened a blank page, and rebuilt the second example himself. It took the whole afternoon. The essay changed less than he feared, but it held together better.

qa.q: Where did Chen write the philosophy essay?
qa.a: He wrote it in the Vancouver public library.

qa.q: What did Chen's wince suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt stung and a little embarrassed that his example assumed what it was trying to prove, even though he had asked for the critique.

qa.q: What else could Chen do to test the rebuilt essay?
qa.a: He could explain the argument aloud to Clara and ask her to push back, since a live objection tests whether the fix really holds.

qa.q: How might Clara view Chen's way of using the tool?
qa.a: Clara might see it as a slower route, but she may notice his essay stays fully his and could try the reviewer approach herself.

grounding: Shows a student drafting first and asking the tool only for gaps in reasoning, then fixing them personally so the work stays theirs.
